newsitem.title: UK: Clarke/George row damages UK inflation credibility.
newsitem.headline: Clarke/George row damages UK inflation credibility.

text.p: The public disagreement between the Bank of England and the Chancellor of the Exchequer over monetary policy is chipping away at Britain's inflation credibility and may push up long-term interest rates and widen gilt/Bund spreads, economists said.

The minutes from the December 11 monetary policy meeting between Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank governor Eddie George, released on Wednesday, showed the rift between the two over interest rates has gaped even wider.
"Fundamentally it is damaging internationally," said Yamaichi cheif economist John Shepperd.
"International investors are likely to shun the UK economy while this wrangling goes on and while the political outlook itself is uncertain."

The minutes said George told the Chancellor interest rates would probably need to rise by half a percentage point in the next few months, particularly if they were left unchanged at 6.0 percent in December, as was the case.
"George has raised the stakes a bit, the debate is warming up," said Morgan Stanley economist Kevin Gardiner.
"If George goes into the next meeting (on February 5) asking for a 50 basis point rise in rates...and Clarke resists, it could have a noticeable impact on the long end of the gilt market."
Economists said Britain's inflation credibility could take a knock if politics is seen interfering in the monetary policy process.
"The fact that rates are not higher will ultimately lead people to ask questions about the longer term inflation prospects in the UK and the political nature of the process," said Shepperd.

George's role in the UK's monetary policy process is that of an adviser and the final decision on rates rests with the Chancellor. This leaves a political element to the process which is at odds with that in other leading economies such as Germany and the U.S.
Shepperd said the question mark over Britain's inflation credibility would make it difficult for gilts to keep pace with their German counterparts.

"The political nature in the UK both in terms of monetary policy and the approaching election argues we will see a widening of the gilt/Bund spread in the next 10 months and this debate doesn't help," said Shepperd.
Gardiner agreed there would be a further widening before the long awaited tightening of spreads.
"We think there will be another opportunity to buy gilts at the 200 basis point spread," he said. At 1300 GMT the spread was at 183 basis points.

But Schroders economist David Philpotts said the credibility Clarke has gained in the eyes of the market during his three and a half years as Chancellor would give him some leeway in the current debate.
"We've been here before," he said. "In the past when Clarke's (gone against the governor) he's got away with it so he's earned quite a lot of credibility with the market."
Britain's monetary policy process has become a lot more transparent since the April 1994 decision to publish the minutes of the monetary meetings between Clarke and George.
But the political element to the process will probabaly lead international investors to side with the governor on the interest rate debate, said Shepperd.

"Clarke can point to a good track record, but I suspect most international investors would be more inclined to back a central banker than a politician who is facing an election within four months," he said.
